body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Serious illness conversation prompts and documented goals-of-care discussions on medical wards: a cluster randomised trial","authors":"Oyelowo-Bergman A, Castillo-Faraday N, Iwu-Hendricks M","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Hospital Palliative Care","doi":"10.5555/jhpc.2019.0415","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomly allocated 12 medical wards to electronic prompts for serious illness conversations with a 90-minute clinician training session, or to usual care. Among 1,480 patients who met prognostic triggers, documented goals-of-care discussions before the last week of life rose from 18 to 41 percent on intervention wards and were unchanged on control wards. Documentation happened a median of 19 days earlier. The trial did not assess the content of the notes and did not measure whether care matched patients' stated goals. Staff on intervention wards reported that the prompts added about four minutes per eligible patient."},{"title":"Tick-box documentation after an electronic advance care planning template: a content analysis of hospital notes","authors":"Lindgren-Oduya S, Pacheco-Wren T","year":2022,"venue":"Palliative Care Documentation Studies","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We analysed 400 advance care planning notes written in the year before and the year after a hospital introduced a structured electronic template. The number of notes rose sharply after the template, but 63 percent of notes contained only resuscitation status and 12 percent documented anything about the patient's values or priorities. On a six-point quality score, the mean was 2.1 before and 2.3 after the template. Notes written by palliative care clinicians scored higher than those written by ward teams. The authors conclude that templates can increase the number of notes without improving what they say."},{"title":"A structured template with ward training and the quality of documented advance care planning conversations: a before-after study","authors":"Achterberg-Nkosi J, Rowan-Takeda L, Faris-Olsen D","year":2021,"venue":"End of Life Care Quality","doi":"10.5555/elcq.2021.0098","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On four medical wards we introduced a structured conversation template together with a 60-minute communication skills session and monthly feedback on note quality. Documentation of advance care planning conversations for patients meeting prognostic triggers rose from 21 to 47 percent over nine months. Two trained raters scored a random sample of notes on a six-point quality scale; the mean quality score rose from 1.8 to 3.9 of 6, with the largest gains in documenting patient values and what matters most. The study had no concurrent comparison, and raters knew the period of each note."},{"title":"Interventions to improve advance care planning documentation in hospital: a systematic review","authors":"Mbeki-Sorensen K, Haddad-Pryce E, Olawale-Lund F","year":2017,"venue":"Supportive and Palliative Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/spcr.2017.0231","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We searched five databases for studies of interventions to increase documented advance care planning among hospital inpatients and included 23 studies. Documentation improved in 17 studies, most often after electronic prompts or templates combined with education. Only 5 studies assessed the quality of documentation and only 3 measured whether care received matched patients' documented preferences, with inconsistent results. Most studies were uncontrolled before-after comparisons at single sites. The review recommends that future evaluations measure the content of conversations and patient-centred outcomes, not documentation alone."},{"title":"Regional review of advance care planning documentation in acute hospitals","authors":"Regional End of Life Care Network","year":null,"venue":"Regional network report series","providerType":"report","abstract":"This network report reviewed the notes of patients who died in 14 acute hospitals in the region. The median proportion with a documented advance care planning conversation before the last week of life was 19 percent, ranging from 8 to 37 percent between hospitals. Five hospitals used a structured template; their median was 24 percent. Data were collected by local staff with different definitions, and the report does not state the period covered or its year of publication. It recommends a common definition and a quality measure for documented conversations."},{"title":"Inter-rater reliability of a six-point quality score for documented serious illness conversations","authors":"Grant-Oyelaran P, Kimura-Bassey R","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Palliative Care Measurement","doi":"10.5555/jpcm.2024.0052","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two palliative care nurses independently rated 150 documented serious illness conversations on a six-point quality score covering prognosis, values, fears, trade-offs, family involvement and recommendations. Before training, agreement was moderate (kappa 0.48). After a two-hour calibration session with worked examples, agreement rose to kappa 0.71. Rating took a median of 6 minutes per note. Notes that recorded only resuscitation status were rated consistently low. The authors recommend calibration and double rating of a sample when the score is used to evaluate an intervention."},{"title":"Bereaved family members' views of end-of-life care planning in hospital: a postal questionnaire study","authors":"Omondi-Castellano R, Wexler-Achebe H","year":2023,"venue":"Family Perspectives in Palliative Care","doi":"10.5555/fppc.2023.0117","providerType":"cross-sectional study","abstract":"We sent a postal questionnaire to the next of kin of 600 patients who died in two hospitals, three to six months after the death. The response rate was 34 percent, lower among families of younger patients and in deprived neighbourhoods. Families who recalled a conversation about goals of care more often reported that care matched the patient's wishes (72 percent compared with 51 percent). Families valued being included in conversations and wanted clearer explanations of what treatments would and would not do. Non-response limits how far the results apply to all bereaved families."}]}
